dependency: Break the preferred operating dependency that a refresh immediately before every commit is necessary for reliable correction: retain the stipulated row-bound editor, perform all three commits on the initially loaded S0 without intermediate refreshes, and refresh only after the commits for final freshness. This directly omits the named dependency; it does not substitute refreshes inside inspection or reinstall it through a correction loop.

predictions.account: Necessity account: reliable, latest-compliant correction requires a refresh immediately before each commit.
predictions.when: Replay the broken-dependency schedule from all-unchecked S0: inspect/select K2 in minutes 0-1 and commit in 1-2; inspect/select K5 in 2-3 and commit in 3-4; inspect/select K7 in 4-5 and commit in 5-6; refresh in 6-7 to load S2. Do not refresh between selection and any commit. Log action times, loaded snapshots, selected rows, intended keys, actual written keys and final statuses.
predictions.result: This necessity account predicts that omitting its prerequisite prevents the valued outcome, despite final freshness. A completed replay with actual writes K2, K5 and K7 only, the exact target status map, loaded S2 and elapsed time seven minutes would falsify that necessity claim within this synthetic model. No such replay is claimed as already observed.

predictions.account: Selection-reordering account: changing the snapshot between row selection and commit causes the stipulated wrong-target write; per-commit freshness is not necessary when target identity is fixed.
predictions.when: Run the same seven-minute schedule with the original row binding. Snapshot eligibility advances at minutes 2 and 5, but S0 remains loaded through all three commits; only the final refresh loads S2, after the last write.
predictions.result: The model predicts the selected rows remain 2, 5 and 7 until their respective commits, so actual writes are K2, K5 and K7, with zero incorrect-key writes. The final refresh reorders the display while preserving local statuses by key, yielding precisely K2, K5 and K7 checked and the other five unchecked. This would preserve the valued outcome while breaking the preferred dependency; it is a prospective prediction derived from stipulated rules, not additional observed causal evidence.

predictions.account: Score-identity account: reading the latest score is sufficient to identify a correction target.
predictions.when: After the final S2 refresh, inspect the displayed keys and status map without performing another commit. Compare identification by score alone with identification by immutable key, particularly for K5 and K7.
predictions.result: The stipulated equal score 75 makes score-only identification ambiguous for K5 and K7. Key inspection predicts an unambiguous final correctness check. The boundary supports using keys for verification but does not establish that every commit requires fresh scores or that repeated mismatch feedback has occurred.

surviving_outcome: Proposed synthetic counterexample: with S0 initially loaded, three sequential inspect/select-and-commit pairs cost six minutes and write checked only to K2, K5 and K7; a single final refresh during minutes 6-7 loads S2 and preserves those local statuses by key. No refresh occurs before any commit. Under the stipulated rules, the predicted surviving outcome is all and only the three target keys checked, no incorrect-key write, unchanged read-only scores, final latest-snapshot compliance and completion within ten simulated minutes. Success remains a hypothesis pending the declared replay; the supplied observed trace establishes one wrong-target write under selection followed by refresh, not necessity of refresh before every commit or repeated feedback. The outcome concerns the eight invented records only.
unknowns: The proposed seven-minute counterexample has not been supplied as an executed trace; actual write logs and final snapshot/status verification are needed to record replay success.
Whether a real editor binds selection to a row or an immutable key is unknown; the attack relies on the stipulated row-bound behavior and key-persistent local statuses.
Real detection rates, interruption costs and usability effects are absent; seven minutes uses only the deterministic simulated action costs.
Concurrent status changes, deleted keys and snapshot-load failures are outside the model, so the counterexample does not establish operational reliability.
The single stipulated miswrite does not demonstrate a repeated mismatch-refresh feedback process; no completed correction trace is supplied.
